title: Peyman Milanfar (@docmilanfar)
summary:
The simplest things in statistics can be deceiving. Let
𝐲 = θ + σ e
where e ~ 𝒩(0,𝐈) is d-dim. You’d think the maximum-likelihood would be good estimate of θ, but you’d be wrong.
James-Stein dominates ML in the mean² sense - as long as d ≥3
Counterintuitively, Stein's estimator "shrinks" the ML towards the origin - away from the data!
By shrinking, it reduces variance -and this more than compensates for the small bias introduced, leading to lower MSE

summary:
The advice to limit blue light before bed targets specific retinal cells: intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs).
Discovered in the early 2000s - these are distinct from rods/cones. They help regulate your body clock using a pigment called melanopsin.
Melanopsin is highly sensitive to blue light wavelengths common in screens and LEDs. Evening exposure activates these cells, sending an erroneous "daytime" signal that suppresses the sleep hormone melatonin, thus interfering with sleep onset.

According to a Coordinator on Problem 6, the one problem OpenAI couldn't solve, "the general sense of the IMO Jury and Coordinators is that it was rude and inappropriate" for OpenAI to do this.
OpenAI wasn't one of the AI companies that cooperated with the IMO on testing their models, so unlike the likely upcoming Google DeepMind results, we can't even be sure OpenAI's "gold medal" is legit. title: Peyman Milanfar (@docmilanfar)
summary:
It's Fall of 1993, around 2:30 AM on a Friday. A ringing phone shatters the quiet of my MIT grad student apartment. My girlfriend (now wife) answers, her face draining of color as she hands me the phone. A young woman's voice, choked with sobs, is asking for me.
Confused, I learn it's a student from a notoriously tough MIT course I'm TA'ing. She's failing, again. This attempt is her last chance to graduate. Her admission to Harvard B-School is on the line. Panic washes over me -I'm just a 20-something TA, what can I do?
But I listen. For an hour, I try to soothe her fears, offering what little guidance I can. She hangs up, calmer. Days later, we grade her final with bated breath. It's close, but she passes. She graduates. She gets into HBS.
Today, she's a powerhouse Silicon Valley entrepreneur, founder, and VC. A success story you'd never guess had such a precarious start. This taught me that you never know the full story behind someone's achievements.
So listen:
* Success isn't linear.
* It's always okay to ask for help.
* Don't give up easily.
* And the best lesson, for me:
It's OK to be kind and compassionate any time of day or night - even at 2:30AM when your wife might think you’re having an affair.

“It has been pointed out elsewhere that if we accept the assertion that real-world images with 𝑁 pixels are approximately contained in low-dimensional manifolds of ℝ^𝑁 , then adding noise is equivalent to orthogonal perturbation away from the manifold, and denoising is approximately a projection onto the manifold. In particular, for small noise, denoising is precisely a projection onto the local tangent of said manifold. As such, the work of denoising is essentially analogous to manifold learning.”

linked_urls.title: The Diffusion Process as a Correlation Machine: Linear Denoising Insights | OpenReview
linked_urls.summary: Recently, diffusion models have gained popularity due to their impressive generative abilities. These models learn the implicit distribution given by a training dataset, and sample new data by transforming random noise through the reverse process, which can be thought of as gradual denoising. In this work, to shed more light on the evolution of denoisers in the reverse process, we examine the generation process as a ``correlation machine'', where random noise is repeatedly enhanced in correlation with the implicit given distribution. To this end, we explore the linear case, where the optimal denoiser in the MSE sense is known to be the PCA projection. This enables us to connect the theory of diffusion models to the spiked covariance model, where the dependence of the denoiser on the noise level and the amount of training data can be expressed analytically, in the rank-1 case. In a series of numerical experiments, we extend this result to general low rank data, and show that low frequencies emerge earlier in the generation process, where the denoising basis vectors are more aligned to the true data with a rate depending on their eigenvalues. This model allows us to show that the linear reverse process is a generalization of the prevalent power iteration method, where the generated distribution is composed of several estimations of the given covariance, in varying stages of convergence. Finally, we empirically demonstrate the applicability of our findings beyond the linear case, in the Jacobians of a deep, non-linear denoiser, used in general image generation tasks.

title: Peyman Milanfar (@docmilanfar)
summary:
Two basic ideas seem true:
1. Talent buys time
2. Talent multiplies practice
- If you can sample wide interests as a kid, start relatively late on a specialization, and still succeed, you are very likely to be gifted. Think Federer or Einstein
- If you are an average kid, specialization is a way to keep up. It masks a lack of raw talent with the compounding effect of practice. It often leads to strong competence; but rarely greatness. No amount of early piano lessons will make an average talent into a Mozart
- But when the truly gifted kids specialize early, specialization becomes rocket fuel for their natural talent. It’s how you get GOATs like Yo-Yo Ma and Messi

Dear friends, I’m excited to share our final and most ambitious AI arts project for 2025 — Machine Dreams: Biophilia, commissioned by Google for their new headquarters, Gradient Canopy.
The project began nearly two years ago to support Large Nature Model research. To create this work, Refik Anadol Studio collected 2 petabytes of audio and imagery from four distinct California biomes by traveling through the Redwoods, Ocean, Bay, and Foothills. It was combined with publicly available ecological datasets to train our Large Nature Model (LNM) sustainably in Google Cloud using renewable energy.
Local weather data from each biome is used in real time to generate text prompts in the latest Gemini, guiding the LNM’s exploration of the datasets. As the weather changes, so do the dreamed images and evolving soundscapes, reflecting nature’s constant motion—a living AI Data Painting that harmonizes perfectly with nature. The breakthrough technology behind the artwork will also power Dataland, and I cannot wait to share more soon. I am deeply grateful to the team that worked so hard on this epic and unique project, and to Google Leadership and scientists for their ongoing support of our studio since 2015!

title: Peyman Milanfar (@docmilanfar)
summary:
Yes
Quoting @kareem_carr
"Is measure theory useless for non-mathematicians?"
After many years of searching, I finally found the answer in this book. Measure theory lets you:
1. Unify the language of continuous and discrete distributions. This saves time since you don't have to repeat arguments to cover both cases.
2. Unify the language of single and multiple variables. This also saves time for the same reason.
3. Define independence of random variables more cleanly.
The usual way independence is taught works well for concrete examples, but once you start reasoning about independence in the abstract, it's easy to lean on intuition in ways that aren't fully precise.
Measure theory gives a single, unambiguous definition that avoids those ambiguities.
4. Define convergence more completely in the statistical context. This makes proofs of convergence shorter and more reliable.
These are strong reasons for statistical theorists, but most applied people probably don't need it.
To be clear, I have taken several courses in measure theory, but it always seemed like insane levels of overkill for my own research.
I always felt like maybe there was something I was missing. This book finally put the pieces together for me.

In 1979, the Imperial Army faced a stark choice. At the height of the crisis, they could have unleashed a civil war that would have turned Iran into a slaughterhouse, or they could step aside. On February 11, they chose to stand down.
Fundamentally, those officers prioritized the survival of the nation over the monarchy; they refused to massacre their own people. But the aftermath was telling. The new regime responded to that restraint with a campaign of retribution, executing not only the very officers who had refused to fire, but effectively waging war on the population itself. In the bloody decade that followed, thousands of political prisoners, students, and ordinary citizens who dared to oppose their ideology were systematically imprisoned and eliminated.
The contrast today is devastating, but unsurprising. The current regime has likely killed more civilians in the first two weeks of this year than the Imperial Army killed during the entire revolutionary struggle of 1978–79. This regime built the IRGC for a different purpose: not to defend Iran and its people from foreign enemies, but to defend their ideology from Iranians. We are no longer seeing a force that steps back to save the country; we are seeing an ideological militia unleashing fire on protesters, turning the nation into the very slaughterhouse that the army of 1979 refused to create.

So the story goes that Iran was ruled by Zahhak, an evil tyrant who had two snakes growing from his shoulders that required a daily meal of human brains. For decades, the country lived in terror as young men were sacrificed to feed the snakes.
One day, Kaveh, a simple blacksmith who had already lost several sons to the snakes, marched into the tyrant court when his last remaining son was arrested. Zahhak, trying to maintain a facade of justice, released the son but asked Kaveh to sign a document attesting to the King's "justice" and "mercy." Kaveh read the document, tore it into pieces in front of the court, and marched out.
He took off his leather blacksmith's apron, placed it on a spear, and used it as a banner to rally the people. This apron, the Derafsh-e Kaviani, became the symbol of Iranian independence and resistance against tyranny.

title: Peyman Milanfar (@docmilanfar)
summary:
Statistical "degrees of freedom" (df) is often conflated with the # of parameters, especially when comparing two models built for the same task. df can help compare two models for the same task that have different number of parameters
The df for any 1-1 (‘image-to-image’) model
𝐟(y) : ℝⁿ → ℝⁿ
is the trace of its Jacobian:
df = div[ 𝐟(y) ] = Trace[ ∇ 𝐟(y) ]
Computing the degrees of freedom is non-trivial, but can be very useful. A nice paper on the topic is this classic from the signal processing community.

title: Peyman Milanfar (@docmilanfar)
summary:
“Why Diffusion Models Don't Need Noise Conditioning”
The current problem is that diffusion models usually need to be told the noise level t at every step, otherwise the same blurry input could mean “slightly noisy real image” or “pure static”, and the right denoising move is really different.
This paper shows that a “blind” model doesn’t actually need chase the score for a specific t. Instead, it can learn one overall landscape that mixes all noise levels together.
You don’t need to hand the model the noise schedule because the geometry of noisy points already “leaks” the noise scale. With the right parameterization, velocity/flow targets stay bounded and stable, while standard noise-prediction can amplify small errors and catastrophically fail.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HCGxXQIXMAAPkYZ.jpg

title: Peyman Milanfar (@docmilanfar)
summary:
> Daily Paper Reading (5/n)
> Topic: Intersection of diffusion models and recurrent depth models (Math Alert)
>
What geometric and dynamical consequences arise when the precise conditional field f(u, t) is replaced by its autonomous posterior average f(u) (Eq. 6 and 7) (a diffusion model without explicit noise level conditioning) ?
In this paper, the authors first highlight two potential issues with this autonomous form:
> How can the model determine which noise level to apply to a given input without explicit conditioning?
> As t -> 0, the energy gradient may become singular, making stable optimization infeasible and thereby preventing convergence to valid data.
This paper answer both questions through a cool decomposition supported by mathematical proofs.
See figures below!
----
Personal Notes:
> A key difference between diffusion models and iterative or recurrent depth models is the presence of explicit meta conditioning, especially noise level injection. This paper shows that such conditioning is not strictly necessary, if the target parameterization is chosen properly. But it does not mean autonomous models are categorically better than conditioned ones.
> This leaves a more interesting follow up question for our line of work: if autonomous models are viable, what do we actually gain by removing diffusion style conditioning? Simplicity alone is not enough: when should we remove explicit conditioning, and what do we gain when we do?
> Respect for the work with insightful theoretical analysis ......

title: Peyman Milanfar (@docmilanfar)
clean_title: Career advice and societal reflections from Peyman Milanfar
summary:
Career "advice":
Live modestly, save money
Put your family and health first
Keep learning -don't live on your laurels
No jerks: don't work for 'em, don't hire 'em
Quoting @deedydas
The vibes in SF feel pretty frenetic right now. The divide in outcomes is the worst I've ever seen.
Over the last 5yrs, a group of ~10k people - employees at Anthropic, OpenAI, xAI, Nvidia, Meta TBD, founders - have hit retirement wealth of well above $20M (back of the envelope AI estimation).
Everyone outside that group feels like they can work their well-paying (but <$500k) job for their whole life and never get there.
Worse yet, layoffs are in full swing. Many software engineers feel like their life's skill is no longer useful. The day to day role of most jobs has changed overnight with AI.
As a result,
1. The corporate ladder looks like the wrong building to climb.
Everyone's trying to align with a new set of career "paths": should I be a founder? Is it too late to join Anthropic / OpenAI? should I get into AI? what company stock will 10x next? People are demanding higher salaries and switching jobs more and more.
2. There’s a deep malaise about work (and its future).
Why even work at all for “peanuts”? Will my job even exist in a few years? Many feel helpless. You hear the “permanent underclass” conversation a lot, esp from young people. It's hard to focus on doing good work when you think "man, if I joined Anthropic 2yrs ago, I could retire"
3. The mid to late middle managers feel paralyzed.
Many have families and don't feel like they have the energy or network to just "start a company". They don't particularly have any AI skills. They see the writing on the wall: middle management is being hollowed out in many companies.
4. The rich aren’t particularly happy either.
No one is shedding tears for them (and rightfully so). But those who have "made it" experience a profound lack of purpose too. Some have gone from <$150k to >$50M in a few years with no ramp. It flips your life plans upside down. For some, comparison is the thief of joy. For some, they escape to NYC to "live life". For others still, they start companies "just cuz", often to win status points. They never imagined that by age 30, they'd be set. I once asked a post-economic founder friend why they didn't just sell the co and they said "and do what? right now, everyone wants to talk to me. if i sell, I will only have money."
I understand that many reading this scoff at the champagne problems of the valley. Society is warped in this tech bubble. What is often well-off anywhere else in the world is bang average here.
Unlike many other places, tenure, intelligence and hard work can be loosely correlated with outcomes in the Bay. Living through a societally transformative gold rush in that environment can be paralyzing. "Am I in the right place? Should I move? Is there time still left? Am I gonna make it?" It psychologically torments many who have moved here in search of "success".
Ironically, a frequent side effect of this torment is to spin up the very products making everyone rich in hopes that you too can vibecode your path to economic enlightenment.
clean_summary: Peyman Milanfar shares advice to live modestly, prioritize family and health, keep learning, and avoid toxic colleagues. He discusses the stark divide in outcomes in Silicon Valley, where a small elite has accumulated vast wealth, while many others feel stuck, uncertain about their careers amid AI-driven changes. Layoffs, job insecurity, and the shifting landscape of work create a sense of paralysis among middle managers and a loss of purpose even among the wealthy. The environment fosters anxiety about whether one is in the right place or if there is still time to succeed, leading many to pursue new products and ventures in hopes of finding their own path to wealth and fulfillment.

title: Peyman Milanfar (@docmilanfar)
clean_title: Jacobian of denoisers governs diffusion model dynamics and sampling efficiency
summary:
Applying a denoiser twice is essentially applying it once, minus a correction term driven by the residual (the score) and steered by the denoiser’s Jacobian. If you drop the noise level by ε between steps, standard diffusion also adds a temporal drift term:
f (f (x, α), α) ≈ f (x, α) - Jₓ(f) [x − f (x, α)] - [∂f/∂α] ε
The diffusion literature is largely an exercise in controlling these two terms. The Jacobian term is the most geometrically consequential - its spectrum dictates the directions the score can move across the manifold from one step to the next.
To keep the drift term negligible, standard solvers take tiny steps. Flow matching bypasses this by enforcing straight-line trajectories, neutralizing the drift term and reducing the residual to a constant velocity vector. This is what enables high-fidelity sampling in just a few steps.
Quoting @docmilanfar
Highly under-appreciated fact: Jacobian of your denoiser is the most mathematically consequential part of a diffusion model. Architecture gets all the attention, but the Jacobian governs everything - even if standard training methods mean you never actually have to look at it
clean_summary: Applying a denoiser twice is effectively the same as applying it once, with an adjustment driven by the residual and the Jacobian of the denoiser. When reducing the noise level between steps, diffusion models include a drift term influenced by the Jacobian spectrum, which determines how the score can move across the data manifold. To keep this drift negligible, standard solvers use tiny steps, but flow matching techniques enforce straight-line trajectories, neutralizing the drift and enabling high-fidelity sampling in fewer steps. The Jacobian of the denoiser is a crucial mathematical component that governs the model's behavior and efficiency, yet it often receives less attention than the architecture itself.

It’s a pity the Higgs boson’s deep impact hasn’t been communicated better. Its significance lies not in surprise, but in providing overwhelming evidence that the vacuum of our Universe behaves like a superconductor, permeated by a field that breaks a fundamental symmetry of nature and influences the forces within it.

The discovery is comparable to Democritus’s ancient idea of atoms, which was revolutionary despite being long theorized before experimental confirmation. The Higgs represents a similar moment of scientific breakthrough.
